items.title: L11: Nested logic: IF, IFS and SWITCH
items.source: Microsoft Support: IF, IFS and SWITCH functions
items.body:
Nested logic lets one formula choose between several outcomes. This formula reads days open in A2: =IF(A2<=5,"Green",IF(A2<=10,"Amber","Red")). It returns Green for 5 or fewer, Amber for 6 to 10 and Red above 10. Excel evaluates the tests from the left and stops at the first one that is TRUE, so order matters. If the tests were reversed, with A2<=10 first, a case open 3 days would be called Amber, because 3 is also at most 10. With upper limits, put the narrowest test first. If the final value_if_false is left out, IF returns the word FALSE rather than a blank.

IFS does the same without nesting: =IFS(A2>10,"Red",A2>5,"Amber",A2>=0,"Green"). It has no built-in "otherwise". If no test is TRUE it returns #N/A, so a value of -1 gives an error. To add a default, finish with a test that is always true, such as TRUE,"Check".

SWITCH compares one expression with exact values: =SWITCH(B2,"E","Escalate","C","Close","Unknown"). A final unpaired argument is the default. Without it, an unmatched value returns #N/A. SWITCH cannot test ranges such as ">10".

An empty cell counts as 0 in a comparison, so a blank days-open cell would be shown as Green and could hide missing data. Guard it with =IF(A2="","Missing",...). Excel allows up to 64 nested IF levels, but long nests are hard to check. When there are many bands, or they change often, use a lookup table instead.

questions.prompt: A2 holds 6. What does =IF(A2<=5,"Green",IF(A2<=10,"Amber","Red")) return?

options.text: Green
Red
Amber
#N/A

questions.hint: 6 fails the first test but passes A2<=10.

questions.prompt: The tests are reversed: =IF(A2<=10,"Amber",IF(A2<=5,"Green","Red")). A2 holds 3. What comes back?

options.text: Amber
Green
Red
FALSE

questions.hint: The first TRUE test wins, and 3 is at most 10.

questions.prompt: =IFS(A2>10,"Red",A2>5,"Amber",A2>=0,"Green") is used and A2 holds -1. What is the result?

options.text: Green
Red
#N/A
FALSE

questions.hint: No test is TRUE and IFS has no default.

questions.prompt: Which change gives the IFS formula a safe default for unexpected values?

options.text: Add a final argument of "Check" on its own
Wrap each test in IFERROR
Reverse the order of the tests
Add TRUE,"Check" as the last pair

questions.hint: IFS needs a test that is always true to catch the rest.

questions.prompt: =SWITCH(B2,"E","Escalate","C","Close") is used and B2 holds "X". What is returned?

options.text: An empty cell
"Close"
FALSE
#N/A

questions.hint: With no default argument, an unmatched SWITCH value is an error.

questions.prompt: Which job can SWITCH not do?

options.text: Match a status code to a label
Supply a default for unmatched codes
Compare against text values
Return a label for any value over 10

questions.hint: SWITCH tests equality only, not ranges.

questions.prompt: The nested IF formula is applied to an empty A2. What does it show, and what is the risk?

options.text: Green, which can hide missing data
Red, because blanks are errors
An error value, which warns the user
Amber, because blank is between the bands

questions.hint: A blank behaves as 0 in comparisons.

questions.prompt: Someone writes =IF(A2>10,"Red",IF(A2>5,"Amber")) and A2 holds 3. What does it return?

options.text: Green
FALSE
A blank cell
#VALUE!

questions.hint: A missing value_if_false returns FALSE.

questions.prompt: The banding has twelve levels and the thresholds change every quarter. What is the best approach?

options.text: Nest twelve IF functions and edit them each quarter
Keep the bands in a table and use a lookup
Use SWITCH with the twelve thresholds
Type the results by hand

questions.hint: A table is easier to check and update than a long nest.

questions.prompt: Why is it risky to put a wide test such as A2<=10 first in a chain of upper limits?

options.text: It catches values meant for narrower bands
It makes Excel run slowly
It converts the result to text
It stops later tests from being read as numbers

questions.hint: Evaluation stops at the first TRUE.

items.title: L11: Lookup and reference: approximate matches
items.source: Microsoft Support: VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP and LOOKUP functions
items.body:
Lookups often map a number onto a band. Suppose a table in E2:F5 has lower limits in column E and labels in F: 0 is Band 1, 25,000 is Band 2, 40,000 is Band 3 and 60,000 is Band 4. An approximate match finds the largest limit that is less than or equal to the value. So 39,999 is Band 2, 40,000 is Band 3 and 24,999 is Band 1. A value below the smallest limit, such as -5, returns #N/A.

VLOOKUP(A2,E2:F5,2,TRUE) does this, but only if the first column is sorted in ascending order. If it is not, results can be wrong without any error showing. The most dangerous slip is leaving out the fourth argument: VLOOKUP then defaults to approximate match, so an ID lookup can silently return the wrong row. For exact matching, write FALSE or 0.

XLOOKUP defaults to exact match. To band a number, use its match_mode: =XLOOKUP(A2,E2:E5,F2:F5,"Not found",-1). Mode -1 means exact match or the next smaller item, and the table does not need sorting. Mode 1 means exact or next larger. The fourth argument is the text shown if nothing matches, instead of #N/A.

LOOKUP(A2,E2:E5,F2:F5) is an older function that always uses approximate matching and needs sorted data. INDEX with MATCH(A2,E2:E5,1) also works for bands. Because MATCH type 1 needs ascending order and type -1 needs descending order, check the sort order whenever approximate matching is used.

questions.prompt: Using the band table, which label does a value of 39,999 receive?

options.text: Band 3
Band 2
Band 1
#N/A

questions.hint: The match is the largest limit not above the value.

questions.prompt: Which value in the band table returns Band 3?
questions.hint: 40,000 is exactly the Band 3 limit.

questions.prompt: What does a value of -5 return with approximate matching on this table?

options.text: #N/A
Band 1
Band 4

questions.hint: It is below the smallest limit in the first column.

questions.prompt: A colleague omits the fourth argument: =VLOOKUP(A2,E2:F5,2). What is the main danger?

options.text: It returns #REF! because the fourth argument is compulsory
It searches the second column instead of the first one
It uses approximate matching and may return a wrong row silently
It looks only at the first few rows of the table range

questions.hint: The default is TRUE, which is approximate.

questions.prompt: What must be true of the first column for VLOOKUP with TRUE to work reliably?

options.text: It contains only text
It is sorted in ascending order
It has no duplicate values at all
It is formatted as a table

questions.hint: Approximate match relies on sorted limits.

questions.prompt: In =XLOOKUP(A2,E2:E5,F2:F5,"Not found",-1), what does the -1 mean?

options.text: Exact match, or the next smaller item
Search from the last item upwards
Return the previous row's label
Ignore case differences

questions.hint: This match_mode suits banding.

questions.prompt: What does XLOOKUP do by default when match_mode is not given?

options.text: Finds the next smaller item
Finds the next larger item
Treats the data as sorted
Looks for an exact match

questions.hint: Unlike VLOOKUP, its default is exact.

questions.prompt: Why is the "Not found" argument useful?

options.text: It makes the lookup treat upper and lower case differently
It speeds up lookups across very large tables of data
It lets one lookup search across several columns at once
It replaces #N/A with your own message when nothing matches

questions.hint: It is the if_not_found argument.

questions.prompt: Which MATCH type suits an ascending table of lower limits?
questions.hint: Type 1 finds the largest value not above the lookup value.

questions.prompt: The limits table is unsorted and a banding VLOOKUP uses TRUE. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: Every value returns #N/A until the table is sorted
Excel sorts the table automatically before it looks
Some values get the wrong band and no error appears
The formula returns the first label for every row

questions.hint: Approximate matching assumes order.

items.title: L11: SUMPRODUCT with conditions
items.body:
SUMPRODUCT multiplies matching items in arrays and adds the results. It can also apply conditions. Take five rows. Region (A2:A6) is N, N, S, S, N. Units (B2:B6) are 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Unit price (C2:C6) is 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

=SUMPRODUCT(B2:B6,C2:C6) gives 10x2 + 20x3 + 30x4 + 40x5 + 50x6 = 700. To total only region N, add a test: =SUMPRODUCT((A2:A6="N")*B2:B6*C2:C6). The test gives TRUE or FALSE for each row, and multiplying converts them to 1 or 0. Region N rows give 20 + 60 + 300 = 380. Region S gives 120 + 200 = 320.

If you write the test as a separate comma-separated argument, such as =SUMPRODUCT((A2:A6="N"),B2:B6), the TRUE and FALSE values are treated as zero, so the result is 0. Either multiply the arrays or convert them with a double minus: =SUMPRODUCT(--(A2:A6="N"),B2:B6), which gives 10 + 20 + 50 = 80.

Conditions combine in two ways. Multiplication means AND: (A2:A6="N")*(B2:B6>15) selects rows that are region N and over 15 units, giving 2 rows. Addition means OR: (A2:A6="S")+(B2:B6>45) can give 2 for a row that meets both, so wrap the sum in a test such as >0 if you only want to count rows once.

All arrays must be the same size, or SUMPRODUCT returns #VALUE!. SUMIFS is faster for simple cases, but SUMPRODUCT handles tests that SUMIFS cannot, such as a calculation inside the test.

questions.prompt: What is =SUMPRODUCT((A2:A6="N")*B2:B6*C2:C6) for the data described?
questions.hint: Only rows 2, 3 and 6 are region N: 20 + 60 + 300.

questions.prompt: What does =SUMPRODUCT(B2:B6,C2:C6) return?
questions.hint: It is the sum of units times price for all five rows.

questions.prompt: What does =SUMPRODUCT((A2:A6="N"),B2:B6) return, written with a comma?

options.text: 80 as a text value
#VALUE!

questions.hint: Booleans in a separate argument are treated as zero.

questions.prompt: What does =SUMPRODUCT(--(A2:A6="N"),B2:B6) return?
questions.hint: The double minus turns TRUE and FALSE into 1 and 0.

questions.prompt: How many rows does =SUMPRODUCT((A2:A6="N")*(B2:B6>15)) count?
questions.hint: Only 20 and 50 units are in region N and above 15.

questions.prompt: What does multiplying two condition arrays achieve?

options.text: OR, since either gives 1
AND, since both must be TRUE for a 1
A count of the FALSE rows
A comparison of totals

questions.hint: 1 times 0 is 0.

questions.prompt: Why can an OR built by adding conditions overcount rows?

options.text: Addition ignores the first array
FALSE is converted to 1
SUMPRODUCT only reads numeric columns
A row meeting both conditions scores 2

questions.hint: Wrap the total in >0 if you only want to count rows once.

questions.prompt: One range is A2:A6 and another is B2:B7. What is the likely result?

options.text: The extra row is ignored
A partial total
#VALUE!

questions.hint: The array sizes must match.

questions.prompt: Region N is what share of total value, as a percentage to one decimal place?
questions.hint: 380 divided by 700.

questions.prompt: When would SUMPRODUCT be preferred to SUMIFS?

options.text: When the data has fewer than five rows in total
When every value in the data is text, not numbers
When speed on a very large file matters most
When the test needs a calculation that SUMIFS cannot hold

questions.hint: SUMIFS is faster for simple criteria.

items.title: L11: Dates: EDATE, EOMONTH, DATEDIF and working days
items.source: Microsoft Support: date and time functions
items.body:
Excel stores a date as a whole number of days from a starting point, so subtracting one date from another gives the number of days between them. Calendar days and working days are different. Monday 3 March 2025 to Friday 14 March 2025 is 11 days by subtraction, but NETWORKDAYS counts both end dates and leaves out weekends, so =NETWORKDAYS(3 Mar 2025,14 Mar 2025) returns 10. A holiday list can be given as a third argument: with Friday 7 March in the list, the result is 9.

WORKDAY adds working days to a start date. =WORKDAY(3 Mar 2025,5) returns Monday 10 March 2025, since the 5 working days are Tuesday to Monday. Add a holiday range so bank holidays are skipped.

EDATE moves a date by whole months and keeps the same day where it can. =EDATE(15 Jan 2025,3) is 15 April 2025. When the target month is shorter, it falls back to the last day, so =EDATE(31 Jan 2025,1) is 28 February 2025. EOMONTH returns the last day of a month: EOMONTH(15 Jan 2025,0) is 31 January and EOMONTH(15 Jan 2025,1) is 28 February. To get the first day of the month, use EOMONTH(date,-1)+1.

DATEDIF counts complete units. For 1 January 2024 to 30 June 2025, "m" gives 17 complete months, "y" gives 1 complete year and plain subtraction gives 546 days. DATEDIF has no help screen in Excel, but it still works.

A date typed as text, such as one imported from another system, will not calculate. Dates that left-align or return #VALUE! in a formula are often text. Convert them with DATEVALUE or a Text to Columns step.

questions.prompt: What does =NETWORKDAYS(3 Mar 2025, 14 Mar 2025) return, with no holiday list?
questions.hint: Both end dates count, and the two weekend days are excluded.

questions.prompt: The same NETWORKDAYS call has Friday 7 March 2025 in the holiday list. What does it return?
questions.hint: One working day is removed.

questions.prompt: What does subtracting 3 Mar 2025 from 14 Mar 2025 give?
questions.hint: Subtraction gives calendar days between the dates.

questions.prompt: What date does =WORKDAY(3 Mar 2025,5) return?

options.text: 8 March 2025
7 March 2025
10 March 2025
11 March 2025

questions.hint: Count five working days from Monday 3 March: Tue to Mon.

questions.prompt: What does =EDATE(31 Jan 2025,1) return?

options.text: 3 March 2025
2 March 2025
31 February 2025
28 February 2025

questions.hint: EDATE falls back to the last day of a shorter month.

questions.prompt: Which formula gives the first day of the month containing a date in A2?

options.text: =EOMONTH(A2,0)-30
=EDATE(A2,0)
=EOMONTH(A2,1)-1
=EOMONTH(A2,-1)+1

questions.hint: Last day of the previous month plus one day.

questions.prompt: What does =DATEDIF(1 Jan 2024, 30 Jun 2025,"m") return?
questions.hint: Seventeen complete months have passed.

questions.prompt: A column of imported dates is left-aligned and gives #VALUE! when subtracted. What is the likely cause?

options.text: The workbook is in manual calculation
The dates are stored as text
The dates are before 1900
The cells need a currency format

questions.hint: Text dates do not calculate.

questions.prompt: With a start date of 15 January 2025 and 1 as the months argument, what does EOMONTH return?

options.text: 28 February 2025
31 January 2025
15 February 2025
1 March 2025

questions.hint: The 1 moves the month on by one, then it returns the month end.

questions.prompt: A team's service standard is 10 working days. Which approach best calculates the due date for a case received on a given date in A2?

options.text: =A2+10 (adding ten calendar days)
=EDATE(A2,10) (adding ten whole months)
=NETWORKDAYS(A2,10,HolidayList)
=WORKDAY(A2,10,HolidayList)

questions.hint: WORKDAY skips weekends and listed holidays.

items.title: L11: Data validation: controlling what goes into cells
items.source: Microsoft Support: apply data validation to cells
items.body:
Data validation limits what a user can type into a cell. It is found under the Data tab and is one of the cheapest ways to improve data quality. Common types are: List, which gives a drop-down; Whole number or Decimal, with a minimum and maximum; Date, with an earliest and latest allowed; Text length; and Custom, which uses a formula that must evaluate to TRUE. For example, =COUNTIF($A:$A,A2)=1 in a custom rule stops the same reference number being entered twice in column A.

A list can be typed in, for example Open,Closed,Escalated, or can point at a range. A range held in an Excel Table, or a named range that expands, updates the drop-down when items are added. A dependent drop-down, where a second list changes with the first choice, can be built with INDIRECT and named ranges.

The error alert has three styles. Stop blocks any invalid entry. Warning tells the user that the entry is invalid and lets them choose to keep it. Information shows a message and lets them click OK to keep it. An input message can show guidance when the cell is selected. Choose Stop for fields that must be exact and Warning where exceptions are valid.

Validation has important limits. It does not check values pasted into the cell: pasting overwrites the rule. It does not test data already in the cells when the rule is added, but "Circle Invalid Data" under the Data Validation menu marks those entries. A user can also clear the rule, so protect the sheet where the structure must hold. Validation reduces mistakes but does not replace a checking step.

questions.prompt: Which validation type would stop a reference number being entered twice in column A?

options.text: Custom, using =COUNTIF($A:$A,A2)=1
List, drawn from the existing reference numbers
Whole number between 1 and 1000 in each cell
Text length equal to ten characters in each cell

questions.hint: The custom formula must be TRUE for entry to be accepted.

questions.prompt: An alert style is set to Warning. What happens when a user enters an invalid value?

options.text: They are told, and can choose to keep it
Excel blocks the entry completely
Excel deletes the value silently
Excel replaces it with the nearest valid value

questions.hint: Only Stop blocks entries outright.

questions.prompt: Which alert style should be used for a field that must always hold an exact value?

options.text: Stop
Warning
Information
None, because input messages do the same job

questions.hint: Stop is the only style that blocks invalid entries.

questions.prompt: A user copies a cell from another sheet and pastes it into a validated cell. What is the usual result?

options.text: Excel checks the pasted value against the rule first
The paste is blocked with a Stop message
The rule is kept and the value is checked later
The value goes in and the validation rule is overwritten

questions.hint: Pasting bypasses and replaces validation.

questions.prompt: Data has been entered for months. A new rule is then added. What does Excel do with the existing entries?

options.text: Deletes any that fail the rule
Turns them red automatically
Leaves them alone, but Circle Invalid Data can mark them
Converts them to text

questions.hint: Existing values are not retested.

questions.prompt: How can a drop-down list update automatically when new items are added to the source?

options.text: Retype the items into the rule each time one is added
Base the list on an Excel Table or expanding named range
Switch off the input message for the cell
Sort the source list alphabetically each week

questions.hint: Tables grow when rows are added.

questions.prompt: Which tool builds a second drop-down that depends on a choice in the first?

options.text: SUMPRODUCT with arrays
DATEDIF with a text argument
A pivot table filter
INDIRECT together with named ranges

questions.hint: INDIRECT turns the first choice into a range name.

questions.prompt: What is an input message used for?

options.text: Blocking pasted data
Showing guidance when the cell is selected
Recording who changed the cell
Encrypting the entry

questions.hint: It appears before anything is typed.

questions.prompt: A whole-number rule allows only 1 to 5. Which entry is rejected under a Stop alert?
questions.hint: A decimal is not a whole number.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the value of validation for a shared tracker?

options.text: It cuts typing errors but still needs checking
It guarantees that every entry in the tracker is correct
It replaces the need for a named data owner
It continues to work on any pasted data

questions.hint: Validation cannot catch every error.

items.title: L11: Pivot logic: how a pivot table calculates
items.source: Microsoft Support: create a PivotTable to analyse worksheet data
items.body:
A pivot table summarises a list without formulas. You drag fields into four areas: Rows and Columns set the groups, Values sets what is calculated, and Filters limits which records are included. The source must have a single header row, no blank headers, no merged cells and no blank rows inside it, or the pivot may misread it. Converting the source to an Excel Table means new rows join automatically.

A pivot does not update when the source data changes. Use Refresh, or the option to refresh on opening the file. A new row added outside the source range will not be picked up unless the range is extended.

The calculation chosen for a Values field matters. Excel defaults to Sum if every value in the field is a number, but switches to Count if the field has text or blanks. A pivot showing "Count of Cost" when you expected totals usually means a blank or text entry in that column.

Averages are calculated from the underlying rows. If Team A has two rows with 10 and 20 cases and Team B has one row with 30, the pivot shows Team A average 15, Team B average 30 and a grand total average of 20, which is 60 divided by 3. It is not the average of the group averages (22.5). The same applies to percentage fields: use "Show Values As" for share of total, for example, instead of averaging percentages.

Dates can be grouped by month, quarter or year. Calculated fields do arithmetic on summed fields, so a ratio field is the sum of one divided by the sum of the other. GETPIVOTDATA pulls a value from the pivot into a formula, and it keeps working if the pivot layout changes.

questions.prompt: What is the grand total Average in the pivot with Team A rows 10 and 20, and Team B row 30?
questions.hint: Total 60 divided by 3 rows.

questions.prompt: Why does the grand total differ from the mean of the group averages (15 and 30)?

options.text: The pivot rounds each group average down before combining
It is calculated from all rows, not from the group averages
It leaves out the largest value in each group
It weights the groups by alphabetical order of name

questions.hint: Averages are not averaged.

questions.prompt: A Values field shows "Count of Cost" rather than a sum. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The Cost column holds text or blanks
The pivot has too many rows
The source is an Excel Table
Filters are switched on

questions.hint: Excel defaults to Count when a field has non-numbers.

questions.prompt: A new row is typed below the source range, outside it. What happens when the pivot is refreshed?

options.text: It is added automatically
Refresh produces #REF!
It appears in the Filters area
It is not included until the source range is extended

questions.hint: Pivot ranges are fixed unless the source is a Table.

questions.prompt: What is the simplest way to make a pivot pick up new rows automatically?

options.text: Use the highest number of rows ever expected
Turn off Refresh
Make the source an Excel Table
Merge the header cells

questions.hint: A Table grows when rows are added.

questions.prompt: Which feature on a source range will most reliably break a pivot?

options.text: A date column
A column of numbers
Having 5,000 rows
A blank header cell

questions.hint: Every column needs a header name.

questions.prompt: When does a pivot table update after a source cell is edited?

options.text: Immediately, as with a formula
When it is refreshed
Only when saved
Only when the filters change

questions.hint: A pivot is a snapshot until refreshed.

questions.prompt: What does a calculated field for cost per case calculate?

options.text: The average of each row's cost per case
Sum of cost divided by sum of cases
The count of cost divided by the count of cases
The mean of the group ratios

questions.hint: Calculated fields work on summed fields.

questions.prompt: Why use "Show Values As" with percent of column total instead of averaging a percentage column?

options.text: It is faster to refresh
It removes blank rows
It gives each group's share of the whole correctly
It sorts the groups

questions.hint: Averaging row percentages ignores the size of each row.

questions.prompt: What does GETPIVOTDATA do?

options.text: Refreshes every pivot table in the workbook at once
Pulls a value by field names, so it survives layout changes
Creates a new pivot table from a typed formula
Locks the pivot table against any further edits

questions.hint: It refers to the pivot item, not the cell address.

items.title: L11: Error handling: IFERROR, IFNA and checks
items.source: Microsoft Support: IFERROR, IFNA and AGGREGATE functions
items.body:
Error values tell you something went wrong. Common ones: #DIV/0! for division by zero, #N/A when a lookup finds nothing, #VALUE! for the wrong type of data, #REF! for a deleted reference and #NAME? for an unrecognised name. Handling them is useful, but hiding them carelessly can produce wrong figures.

IFERROR(value, fallback) replaces any error with the fallback. IFNA(value, fallback) replaces only #N/A. Use IFNA with a lookup so that a real fault, such as a deleted column that gives #REF!, still shows and is not disguised as "not found". Wrapping an entire long formula in IFERROR can conceal mistakes you needed to see.

The choice of fallback matters. Suppose =IFERROR(A2/B2,0) is filled down three rows with results 0 (from a zero divisor), 4 and 6. The average of the three is 3.33. If the fallback is "" (empty text) the first cell is skipped by AVERAGE, which gives 5. A zero says "this ratio is zero", but the true answer is "no ratio". Another approach tests the cause: =IF(B2=0,"",A2/B2).

A single error in a range makes SUM return that error. AGGREGATE can ignore errors: =AGGREGATE(9,6,C2:C20) sums the range, where 9 means SUM and 6 means ignore error values. It is better to find and fix the cause than to ignore errors when the output is going into a report.

ISNUMBER, ISTEXT and ISBLANK return TRUE or FALSE and help to check inputs. ISERROR returns TRUE for any error. Build a check cell that counts errors, for instance =SUMPRODUCT(--ISERROR(C2:C20)), and make it show a warning on the summary sheet.

questions.prompt: Which function replaces only #N/A and leaves other error values visible?

options.text: IFERROR
ISERROR
IFNA
AGGREGATE

questions.hint: It is narrower than IFERROR.

questions.prompt: Why is IFNA often safer than IFERROR around a lookup?

options.text: It runs noticeably faster on large workbooks
It returns zero by default instead of blank
A genuine fault such as #REF! stays visible
It works only with exact-match lookups

questions.hint: IFERROR would hide every error type.

questions.prompt: Results of =IFERROR(A2/B2,0) down three rows are 0, 4 and 6. What is their average?
questions.hint: 10 divided by 3.

questions.prompt: The fallback is changed to "" and the results are "", 4 and 6. What does AVERAGE return?

options.text: #VALUE!

questions.hint: AVERAGE ignores text in a range.

questions.prompt: Why can a fallback of 0 be misleading?

options.text: It says the ratio is zero when there was no ratio
It makes the column text
It turns the cell into an error
It stops filtering from working

questions.hint: Zero is a real value.

questions.prompt: What does =AGGREGATE(9,6,C2:C20) do?

options.text: Averages the range
Sums the range and ignores error values
Counts the errors
Returns the largest value

questions.hint: 9 means SUM and 6 means ignore errors.

questions.prompt: A SUM over C2:C20 returns #N/A because one cell has that error. What is the best first response?

options.text: Wrap the SUM in IFERROR so that it returns 0
Delete the row from the sheet and carry on
Find why that cell has #N/A and fix the cause
Format the cell so that the error is not displayed

questions.hint: Ignoring errors can hide wrong totals in a report.

questions.prompt: Which formula checks the range C2:C20 and gives the number of cells with any error?

options.text: =ISERROR(C2:C20)
=COUNTBLANK(C2:C20)
=SUMPRODUCT(--ISERROR(C2:C20))
=IFERROR(C2:C20,0)

questions.hint: ISERROR gives TRUE or FALSE for each cell.

questions.prompt: Which error value usually means a cell that a formula referred to has been deleted?

options.text: #NAME?
#REF!
#DIV/0!
#N/A

questions.hint: The reference no longer exists.

questions.prompt: Which formula avoids the error and leaves a gap when B2 is zero?

options.text: =IFNA(A2/B2,0)

questions.hint: The test must be on the divisor.

items.title: L11: What a formula really returns
items.source: Microsoft Support: ROUND, INT, TRUNC, MOD, COUNTA and COUNTBLANK functions
items.body:
A formula returns a value, but what you see may differ from what is stored. Number formats change the display only. A cell holding 2.5 and formatted with no decimals shows 3, yet a formula adding it to 1 gives 3.5, not 4. ROUND changes the stored value: ROUND(2.5,0) is 3 and ROUND(-2.5,0) is -3, as halves round away from zero. ROUND(1234,-2) is 1200. INT rounds down towards minus infinity, so INT(-2.5) is -3. TRUNC cuts off the decimal part, so TRUNC(-2.5) is -2.

MOD returns the remainder after division, and takes the sign of the divisor. MOD(17,5) is 2 and MOD(-7,3) is 2. QUOTIENT(17,5) returns the whole-number part, 3.

Text and numbers behave differently. A number stored as text, such as "5", is ignored by SUM when it is in a cell range, but is converted if used directly in arithmetic: if A2 holds the text "5", then =A2+5 returns 10 while =SUM(A2) skips it and returns 0. Percent signs are numbers: 50%*200 is 100. TRUE counts as 1 in arithmetic.

An empty-looking cell may not be empty. A formula returning "" produces empty text. ISBLANK on that cell returns FALSE, and COUNTA counts it. COUNTBLANK counts both truly empty cells and cells holding "". This is why a count of "non-blank" entries can exceed the number of visible entries.

Comparisons are not case-sensitive: "a"="A" is TRUE. The EXACT function is case-sensitive. Check what a formula returns with Evaluate Formula, or by typing it into a spare cell, before relying on it.

questions.hint: INT rounds down towards minus infinity.

questions.hint: TRUNC just removes the decimal part.

questions.hint: It returns the whole-number part of the division.

questions.hint: COUNTBLANK includes empty text.

questions.hint: A negative digit count rounds to the left of the decimal point.

items.title: L11: Briefing a senior reader: structure
items.source: GOV.UK: Civil Service Success Profiles, Communicating and Influencing; departmental briefing guidance
items.body:
A briefing helps a senior reader decide or act, usually in minutes. Put the point first. Many departments call this the bottom line up front: the first paragraph says what you are asking, what you recommend and by when. Do not make the reader wade through the background to find it.

A common structure, which departments often vary, is: Issue or purpose; Recommendation; Timing; Background; Analysis or Options; Risks; Financial, legal and communications points; Handling; and Annexes. The main text is usually kept to one or two pages, with detail in annexes. Lines to take and Q&A for meetings are separate from the briefing itself.

Write the summary last, because only then do you know what matters. Test it by asking whether the reader could act on it alone. Use short paragraphs, numbered paragraphs for cross-reference and headings that say something: "Costs have risen 12% against budget" tells the reader more than "Finance".

Separate fact, judgement and opinion. Say where figures come from and how reliable they are. If the data is provisional or the sample small, say so near the figure, not in a footnote. Give the reader the risks that matter most and what you are doing about them, not a long list in no order.

A recommendation must be specific and be something the reader can say yes or no to, for example, "Agree to extend the contract for six months at the current rate." Avoid ending with "views welcome". Check names, dates and numbers against sources, and have a colleague read it fresh. Mark the right classification and handling instruction.

questions.prompt: Where should the recommendation normally appear in a briefing for a senior reader?

options.text: After the full background
Only in an annex
In the first paragraph or summary
In the closing paragraph, after the risks

questions.hint: The reader should see the ask immediately.

questions.prompt: What does "bottom line up front" mean?

options.text: Stating the ask and recommendation at the start
Putting the costs in a paragraph at the very end
Listing the least important points first

questions.hint: It saves the reader's time.

options.text: The background

The summary

options.text: Finance

questions.hint: A heading that says something tells the reader the message.

options.text: In a footnote at the end
In the annex only
Nowhere, if the figure is small

questions.hint: The reader must see the caveat when they read the number.

questions.prompt: Which recommendation is best written for a senior reader?

options.text: Consider whether the contract might need to be extended in future
Agree to extend the contract for six months at the current rate

questions.hint: It can be answered yes or no.

options.text: To hide unfavourable facts

questions.hint: Detail goes at the back.

options.text: Alphabetise them

questions.hint: Prioritise for the reader.

questions.hint: It is a forecast, not a measured fact.

questions.prompt: Why use numbered paragraphs?

options.text: To make the briefing look longer
To satisfy a legal rule
To show which paragraphs are classified
So readers can refer to them precisely in a meeting or reply

questions.hint: They make cross-reference easy.

items.title: L11: Writing for ministers and the public
items.source: GOV.UK: Style guide; Civil Service Code; ministerial correspondence guidance
items.body:
Draft replies for ministers are written in the minister's voice. Officials draft the text, the private office reviews it and the minister signs, so it uses "I" and "we" and not "the Department considers". Start with the answer to the question asked or the main point. Thank the person for writing in the first line only, if at all, and avoid phrases such as "I am writing in response to your letter of".

Be accurate and make no commitments that have not been agreed. A reply must not announce new policy, promise money or pre-empt a decision. If the matter is subject to legal proceedings, check with lawyers before drafting. Say what the government is doing and why, in plain English, and give the person something they can use: a link, a number to call, or what to do next. Check that every fact, figure and date is right and that sources are recorded for the private office.

Most readers are not specialists. The GOV.UK style guide asks for plain English: short sentences, active verbs, no jargon and no unexplained acronyms. Use "you" and "we". Say "buy" not "purchase", "help" not "facilitate". Put one idea in a paragraph. Use numbers, not words, for figures, and write dates in full, such as 5 March 2025. Do not use "please find attached"; say what the attachment is.

Tone matters. If the person has had a poor experience, acknowledge it before explaining. Do not use "unfortunately" as a cushion, and do not be defensive. If the answer is no, give the reason and the next step, such as the right to a review or the route of complaint.

Draft in the public's accessible formats too: if a person has asked for large print or easy read, the reply should be provided that way.

questions.prompt: In whose voice is a draft reply for a minister written?

options.text: The Department's, using "the Department"
The minister's, using "I" and "we"
The private office's, using "we have been asked"
The official who drafted it, using "I"

questions.hint: The minister signs it.

questions.prompt: A draft hints that funding will be increased next year, though no decision has been made. What should the drafter do?

Keep it, with the word "may" added to soften it
Move it to the last paragraph so it is less prominent
Keep it, adding that it is not yet formal policy

questions.hint: Replies must not pre-empt decisions.

options.text: Send the standard reply
Check with departmental lawyers

Leave the matter out of the reply

questions.hint: Legal advice may limit what can be said.

questions.hint: It uses plain words, an active verb and a full date.

options.text: It does not say what the attachment is or why it matters

questions.hint: Tell the reader what the attachment is.

questions.prompt: A person reports a poor experience. What should the reply do first?

options.text: Explain the policy in detail

questions.hint: Acknowledging comes first, without promising a remedy.

options.text: A list of every rule that applies

An apology only

questions.hint: The reader needs to know what happens next.

options.text: twelve thousand five hundred people and 5th of March

12.5k people and March 5

questions.hint: Use numerals and write dates in full.

options.text: Send the standard letter with a note

items.title: L11: Minutes, decisions and action logs
items.source: Cabinet Office: guidance on minutes and records; ICO guidance on subject access
items.body:
Minutes record what a meeting decided and who must do what. They are not a transcript. A good record shows the date, attendees and apologies, each decision with a short reason, and each action. Discussion is summarised only enough to make the decision understandable.

A good action has a verb, one named owner and a date. "Draft the options paper" is better than "Options paper", and "Owner: Priya, by 14 March" is better than "Policy team, soon". An action with two owners often has none. If the work is shared, name a lead. Break large tasks into smaller steps that can be closed, and note dependencies, such as "after budget sign-off".

An action log is a live list. At each meeting the chair reviews the open actions first. Record status simply, such as open, due, overdue or closed. Close an action only when it is done, and note what was done and where the evidence is. If an action cannot be met, record the new date and the reason, not a silent change. Repeated overdue items should be raised with the owner's line manager.

Circulate draft minutes soon after the meeting, while memory is fresh, often within two working days, and ask the chair to approve them. Corrections are agreed at the next meeting and the approved version becomes the record. Keep one master copy with version control.

Minutes are official records. They can be disclosed in response to a Freedom of Information request or a subject access request, so write facts and decisions in neutral language. Leave out personal remarks and opinions of individuals, and mark sensitive items clearly.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of minutes?

options.text: To record decisions, reasons and actions
To provide a full transcript of the discussion
To list who attended and who sent apologies
To set the agenda for the next meeting

questions.hint: They are not a transcript.

questions.prompt: Which action is best written?

options.text: Options paper - Policy team - as soon as possible
Someone to take a look at the options paper
Draft options paper - Priya - by 14 March
Options paper discussed and noted by the group

questions.hint: It has a verb, one owner and a date.

questions.prompt: Why is an action with two joint owners a problem?

options.text: It cannot be recorded in a log
Each may assume the other will do it
It breaks data protection rules
It must be agreed by the chair

questions.hint: Name a lead where the work is shared.

questions.prompt: What should the chair usually review first at the next meeting?

options.text: The open actions from the last meeting
Any other business
The date of the next meeting
The agenda for the following quarter

questions.hint: Action review keeps work moving.

questions.prompt: An owner cannot meet a deadline. What should the log record?

options.text: Nothing until the work is done
The new date and the reason
A deleted action
The original date only

questions.hint: Do not change dates silently.

questions.prompt: When should an action be marked closed?

options.text: When it has been done and the evidence is noted
When the meeting ends
When the owner says they will start
When the date passes

questions.hint: Closure needs proof of completion.

questions.prompt: Why should draft minutes be circulated quickly?

options.text: Memory is fresh and errors are easier to correct
So the chair has less time to read the draft
To meet a legal limit of 24 hours for minutes
So attendees can add their own remarks afterwards

questions.hint: A short delay improves accuracy.

questions.prompt: Why must minutes be written in neutral, factual language?

options.text: They are always published on GOV.UK after approval
They may be disclosed under FOI or a subject access request
They are routinely audited by the National Audit Office
They count as legally binding contracts between attendees

questions.hint: Records can be released.

options.text: A remark about a colleague's personal circumstances
A decision to approve the budget
An action with an owner and a date
A reason for deferring the item

questions.hint: Personal remarks and opinions have no place in the record.

questions.prompt: Dependencies in an action log are noted so that

options.text: The chair can remove the action
The action is shown as closed
Two owners can be named
The reader can see what must happen first

questions.hint: They explain why an action may not yet be due.

items.title: L11: UK GDPR: choosing a lawful basis and doing a DPIA
items.source: ICO: Guide to the UK GDPR, lawful basis and data protection impact assessments
items.body:
Before processing personal data, you need a lawful basis under Article 6 of the UK GDPR. There are six: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests. Choose the one that fits the purpose and record why. No basis is better than another, but they have different consequences.

Public authorities usually rely on public task: processing needed to perform a task in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority, which must have a basis in law. Legitimate interests cannot be used by a public authority for tasks it performs as a public authority. Consent is rarely suitable where there is a clear imbalance of power, such as a person who depends on a service, because it must be freely given and can be withdrawn. If you rely on consent, you must be able to prove it and stop when it is withdrawn.

Special category data, such as health, ethnicity or biometric data, also needs a condition under Article 9, as well as an Article 6 basis. Criminal offence data has its own rules too.

A data protection impact assessment (DPIA) is required before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to people. Examples include large-scale use of special category data, systematic monitoring, new technologies and decisions that affect people through automated processing. A DPIA describes the processing, assesses necessity and proportionality, identifies risks to individuals and sets out the measures to reduce them. The data protection officer must be asked for advice. If a high risk remains after mitigation, the ICO must be consulted before the processing starts.

A DPIA is not a one-off form: update it when the processing changes. A manager's job is to make sure it is done early enough to change the design.

options.text: Four
Five
Eight
Six

questions.hint: They run from consent to legitimate interests.

questions.prompt: Which basis do public authorities usually use for their core tasks?

options.text: Legitimate interests
Consent
Vital interests

questions.prompt: What is true of legitimate interests for a public authority?

options.text: It is always the best choice for government work

questions.hint: Public tasks have their own basis.

questions.prompt: A team will process health data. What does it need?

options.text: An Article 9 condition only

questions.hint: Special category data needs both.

options.text: Within a month after the processing has started

options.text: Updating a team's rota

questions.hint: Systematic monitoring and new technology both signal high risk.

options.text: The processing can go ahead with a note on file

options.text: The Cabinet Secretary
The head of procurement
The data protection officer

questions.hint: The DPO advises on the DPIA.

items.title: L11: Records management: retention, disposal and the record
items.source: The National Archives: Records management guidance; Public Records Act 1958; Freedom of Information Act 2000 section 46 Code
items.body:
A record is information created or received in the course of business that is kept as evidence of what was done and why. Not everything is a record. Drafts, duplicates and personal notes are usually not, though a draft can become one if it shows a decision. What matters is the content and function, not the format: email, a message in a chat tool or a document in a shared drive can all be records.

Information that matters should be stored in an approved corporate system with the right access controls, not in a personal mailbox, a personal drive or on a device. Use clear file names and version control, so that the final approved version can be found.

A retention schedule says how long each type of record is kept and what happens at the end: destroy, review or transfer. Keep records only as long as there is a business, legal or historical need. The UK GDPR storage limitation principle also means personal data must not be kept longer than necessary for its purpose. Disposal must be authorised, documented and carried out securely. Never destroy information that is the subject of a live FOI request, subject access request or legal hold. Deliberately altering, concealing or destroying information to prevent disclosure after a request is a criminal offence under section 77 of the Freedom of Information Act.

Under the Public Records Act 1958, records selected for permanent preservation are transferred to The National Archives, generally by the time they are 20 years old. Departments decide with the Archives which records have historic value. Others are destroyed under the schedule.

Information asset owners are accountable for the records in their area. Managers should make sure leavers' files are transferred, not deleted, and that handovers include where the records live.

items.title: L11: Accessible documents: Word, PDF and the public sector duty
items.source: GOV.UK: Make your documents accessible; Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations 2018; GDS accessibility guidance
items.body:
A document is accessible if people with different needs can use it, including those using screen readers, magnification, voice control or a keyboard only. The Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) Accessibility Regulations 2018 require public sector websites and apps to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) at level AA, and to publish an accessibility statement. Documents published on a website are covered. The Equality Act 2010 also requires reasonable adjustments.

The best accessibility choice on GOV.UK is often to publish content as a web page (HTML), not as a PDF or Word file. HTML adapts to the user's device and settings. If you do publish a document, build it in Word with the structure in place first.

Use real headings from the Styles gallery, not bold text, so a screen reader can list and jump between sections. Use heading levels in order. Use real bullet and number lists. Write descriptive link text such as "Read the complaints policy", not "click here". Give images alt text that conveys their purpose, or mark purely decorative images as such. Do not put important text inside an image. Do not rely on colour alone: text must have enough contrast with its background, at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text at level AA. Keep tables simple, with a header row marked, and no merged or split cells. Avoid text boxes, floating objects and blank paragraphs used for spacing.

Set the document language and a meaningful title in the properties. Run the Accessibility Checker, but treat it as a start: it cannot tell if alt text is useful or the reading order makes sense. When saving to PDF, use the built-in export so tags are kept, and check the result.

items.title: L11: Using AI tools safely at work
items.source: UK Government: Generative AI Framework for HMG; ICO guidance on AI and data protection
items.body:
Generative AI tools can help with drafting, summarising and ideas, but they bring risks that every civil servant should understand. The government's Generative AI Framework sets out principles including: know what the tools are and what their limits are; use them lawfully, ethically and responsibly; keep them secure; ensure meaningful human control; and follow your organisation's policies.

Know the limits. These tools generate plausible text, not verified facts. They can invent sources, figures and quotations, a problem often called hallucination, and they can reflect bias in their training data. Always check output against reliable sources, and never submit something you cannot explain or defend. You remain responsible for anything you send out under your name, however it was drafted.

Protect information. Do not paste personal data, OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE or higher material, commercially sensitive information or unpublished policy into a public tool, because the input may be stored, used to train the model or seen by the provider. Use only tools your department has approved for the kind of information involved. If you are unsure of the classification, treat the content as sensitive and ask.

Keep humans in charge. Under UK GDPR, people have rights regarding decisions made solely by automated means which have legal or similarly significant effects. A tool must not make or effectively make such a decision about a person's benefits, status or services without a lawful basis and safeguards, including human review. A DPIA is usually needed when a new AI tool processes personal data.

Be open and keep records. If AI materially shaped a document, follow departmental guidance on saying so, and keep the prompts and outputs where they are part of the official record. Report any accidental disclosure as an incident straight away.

questions.prompt: What is a key risk when a generative AI tool produces a citation or a figure?

options.text: It is always copied from a government source
It is stored in the departmental record
It may be invented but look plausible
It is automatically checked

options.text: The tool's provider
The IT department
The person who sent it under their name
Nobody, if the tool was approved

questions.hint: Responsibility stays with the user.

questions.prompt: Which material should not be pasted into a public AI tool?

options.text: A published GOV.UK page
A request for ideas for a team away day
A draft containing personal data from a case
A generic definition of a term

questions.hint: Inputs may be stored or seen by the provider.

questions.prompt: You are unsure of the classification of a document you want summarised by AI. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Treat it as sensitive and ask before using the tool
Use the tool, as the content may be fine
Remove names and use the tool
Use a personal account to be safe

questions.hint: Doubt means treat as sensitive.

questions.prompt: Which tools may be used with government information?

options.text: Any tool with a free tier
Any tool that does not ask for a login
Those the department has approved for that kind of information
Any tool on a personal phone

questions.hint: Approval is by type of data.

questions.prompt: Which UK GDPR right concerns decisions made solely by automated means?

options.text: The right not to be subject to such decisions where they have legal or similarly significant effects
The right to be forgotten in all cases
The right to a free copy of the algorithm
The right to choose the processor

questions.hint: Human review is needed for significant decisions.

questions.prompt: A team plans a tool that scores benefit claims and sends refusals without a person checking them. What is the problem?

options.text: Scoring of claims is banned by law
Refusals of a claim are always unlawful
It needs ministerial consent in every case
It risks a solely automated significant decision without safeguards

questions.hint: Meaningful human control is needed.

questions.prompt: What is usually needed before a new AI tool processes personal data?

options.text: A press notice
A signature from the data subject
Nothing, if the supplier is UK based
A data protection impact assessment

questions.hint: New technology with personal data signals high risk.

questions.prompt: If an AI tool materially shaped a document, what is good practice?

options.text: Say nothing in any circumstances
Follow departmental guidance on disclosure and keep relevant records
Delete the prompts straight away
Credit the tool as the author

questions.hint: Openness and record-keeping are part of responsible use.

questions.prompt: You pasted a case summary containing names into a public tool by mistake. What should you do?

options.text: Report it as an incident straight away
Delete the chat and say nothing
Wait to see if anything happens
Tell the supplier only

questions.hint: Prompt reporting limits harm.
